abstract: |
  The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) cuts an importer's charge by the carbon price the exporter has effectively paid, installation by installation. Two flaws follow. Instruments that send a full price signal but pay little net, such as feebates, rebated carbon taxes and energy subsidy reform, earn no credit. And exporters can ship scrap-based steel to the EU and blast-furnace steel elsewhere, cutting reported embodied carbon by three quarters in a stylized case while global emissions stay the same. Measuring the price signal at country-sector level fixes both. The Commission should publish its default carbon price methodology for consultation and build these changes into the 2027 default-value revision.

*Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.3, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. Legal texts as of 29 October 2026: Regulation (EU) 2023/956 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2025/2083 (Official Journal, 17 October 2025), and the Commission's draft implementing regulation on carbon prices paid in third countries, published for feedback on 13 May 2026.*

# Executive summary {.unnumbered}

**The problem.** From 2026 the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) charges importers of steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, hydrogen and electricity for the carbon embodied in what they buy. The charge falls by any carbon price the exporter has "effectively paid", net of rebates, plant by plant. That rule is right for its first purpose, stopping the same tonne being priced twice. It fails the second, encouraging trading partners to decarbonize, in two ways.

**Recognition.** Most developing countries price carbon, if at all, through fuel taxes, subsidy reform or rebated schemes. None of these leaves a certified payment on an export consignment, so all of them earn nothing. A revenue-neutral feebate is the clearest case: it charges every tonne of emissions above a sector benchmark at the full rate, yet the average producer pays zero net. The Commission's default carbon price, the only route most exporters can reach, still has no published methodology.

**Shuffling.** A steelmaker with blast furnaces and scrap-fed electric arc furnaces can send the scrap-based steel to the EU and sell the rest at home or in third markets. In this brief's stylized case, emissions reported on EU-bound steel fall by 76 percent and the CBAM bill by €102 million a year, while the exporter's emissions do not change. Aluminum made from scrap allows the same move.

**The proposal.** Recognize the price signal, measured across the whole sector of the exporting country, alongside the price paid. A feebate or rebated tax at rate *t* gives every producer the incentive *t* to cut emissions intensity, whichever plant supplies Europe. The Total Effective Carbon Price (TECP) puts that signal, and non-price instruments, on one scale. Exporters with a sector-wide signal should face country-level default values without the punitive mark-up, which leaves nothing to gain from routing.

**Why it works.** A country-sector measure does not depend on which plant shipped the goods, so shuffling earns nothing. A domestic feebate prices all output, not the tenth that reaches Europe.

**What it costs.** The measurement already exists in World Bank, IMF and OECD carbon-pricing data. The cost is the work of building it into CBAM, and some legal drafting: the Regulation admits a default carbon price only where the exporting country has set a carbon price.

**What to do.** The Commission should publish its default carbon price methodology for consultation; phase in recognition of implicit and rebated pricing from 2027 to 2034, matching the free allocation phase-out; confirm that revenue-financed decarbonization support does not reduce the recognized price; guard against offsetting subsidies; and develop the default carbon price and default values together for the December 2027 revision.

# Why it matters

The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), Regulation (EU) 2023/956, entered its definitive period in January 2026 [@EU2023; @EU2025Omnibus]. Importers buy certificates for the carbon embodied in covered goods, and free allocation to EU producers phases out as the charge phases in, reaching the full charge in 2034. The EU will raise or forgo revenue under this design, but its larger effect is on trading partners: whether CBAM pushes them toward carbon pricing, and which instruments it rewards.

The mechanism rests on two measurements. The first is embodied carbon, measured either from verified plant data or from Commission default values set at each exporting country's average emissions intensity plus a mark-up [@EU2025Omnibus, Annex IV, point 4.1]. The second is the carbon price paid abroad, which reduces the number of certificates the importer must surrender [@EU2023, Art. 9]. This brief shows that both measurements work plant by plant, and that this is the source of both flaws. It draws on the author's submission to the Commission's 2026 consultation [@Stretton2026Submission].

# How CBAM credits foreign carbon prices

**The law credits payments, not incentives.** Article 9(1), as amended in October 2025, allows a reduction only "if the carbon price has been effectively paid", and requires "any rebate or other form of compensation" to be taken into account [@EU2025Omnibus]. The documentation must be certified by a person independent of the declarant and of the exporting country's authorities. Where embodied carbon is declared from default values, the only route is a yearly default carbon price, which the Commission "may" determine from 2027, publishing its methodology, but "only where a carbon price was set by the rules applicable in the third country" [@EU2025Omnibus, Art. 9(4)]. The recitals ask for that default to be set "including on a conservative basis" [@EU2025Omnibus, recital 20].

**The draft implementing rules make the plant-level logic explicit.** The draft the Commission put out for feedback in May 2026 builds the price paid up good by good: identify the mechanism, attribute covered emissions to each product, then deduct free allowances, below-baseline credits in baseline-and-credit systems, exemptions, reduced rates, refunds and compensation [@EC2026Draft; @ELP2026]. Subsidies financed from carbon-pricing revenue are not treated as compensation. The certifier must be accredited by a national accreditation body to EN ISO/IEC 17029 [@ELP2026].

**Default values penalize missing data, and they are steep.** For hot-rolled flat steel (CN 7208), the country defaults are 4.28 tCO₂ per tonne for India, 3.19 for China and 2.43 for Türkiye, and 4.05 for countries without reliable data, set at the average of the ten most intensive exporters [@EC2025DefaultValues; @EU2025Omnibus, recital 35]. A mark-up of 10 percent in 2026, 20 percent in 2027 and 30 percent from 2028 applies on top, so India's default rises to 5.56 [@EC2025DefaultValues]. The default-value tables also assign each country and product a production route, which sets the benchmark used to adjust for free allocation. An exporter with plants cleaner than its country default has every reason to file plant data; one with dirtier plants files nothing.

# Four gaps in recognition

**First, the default carbon price has no published methodology.** For a country whose instrument generates no certifiable payment, the default is the only route, and without a stated rule it is effectively zero. That is a policy choice made without being stated. Nothing in the consultation set out how a default would be computed or when [@Stretton2026Submission].

**Second, implicit carbon pricing is invisible.** Fuel excises above efficient levels, the removal of fossil fuel subsidies and administered energy price reform all raise the cost of carbon-intensive production in proportion to emissions. None is a "carbon price" under the Regulation, because none is levied on greenhouse gases as such. Implicit prices can be negative, where fuel is subsidized, and a country moving from subsidy toward taxation bears real fiscal and political costs that the framework cannot see. Measures exist: the World Bank's total carbon price combines explicit prices with fuel taxes net of subsidies [@Agnolucci2024], the IMF estimates subsidies against efficient fuel prices [@Black2023], and the OECD publishes effective carbon rates by country and sector [@OECD2023].

**Third, the price paid is not the price signal.** The price paid answers the level-playing-field question: did this consignment already bear a carbon cost? The price signal, called here the relative carbon price, answers whether the instrument drives decarbonization: how much more a high-carbon tonne costs to produce than a low-carbon one, across the sector. For a flat carbon tax the two coincide. For a revenue-neutral feebate, which charges $t(e_i - \bar e)$ per tonne of output on intensity $e_i$ above the sector benchmark $\bar e$ and rebates below it [@CFPB12], they diverge completely. The signal is the full rate $t$; the average producer pays nothing net, and every producer below the benchmark receives money. Output-based rebating of a carbon tax is the same instrument [@KeenParryRoaf2022]. Under the draft, the rebate is netted off and recognition falls to zero. The rule therefore penalizes the design most likely to pass in a large emitter, because returning the revenue is what makes a carbon price politically survivable [@CFPB11].

**Recognition should follow economic incidence, not the share that crosses the EU border.** Suppose a carbon tax with a gross bill of 20 percent of steel production costs, its revenue returned as support for decarbonization, cuts emissions intensity by a fifth. Using the cost formula in @CFPB11, net costs rise by about half the intensity cut times the tax bill, 2 percent (stylized). That cost falls on all output. If a tenth goes to the EU, crediting only the EU slice captures a tenth of the burden the country has accepted.

**Fourth, a nominal carbon price looks the same as a real one.** Netting reaches only support delivered inside the pricing mechanism. A government can levy a compliant carbon tax and raise general support to the same sector by the same amount; the certifier sees a genuine payment and the economy sees no change. A state-owned steelmaker paying carbon tax to a state that covers its losses moves money within one balance sheet. Countervailing-duty rules under the WTO subsidy agreement could in principle reach such cases, but they run on other timetables, burdens of proof and institutions.

# Scrap and route shuffling

**Plant-level measurement lets exporters lower reported embodied carbon by choosing which plant supplies Europe.** Steel made from scrap in an electric arc furnace (scrap-EAF) emits a fraction of steel made from iron ore in a blast furnace and basic oxygen furnace (BF-BOF): about 0.3 against 2.2 tCO₂ per tonne of direct emissions [@IEA2020]. A producer with both can direct the scrap-based output to the EU and keep selling blast-furnace steel elsewhere. The verifier certifies, accurately, what it is shown. Sandbag's scenarios for imports from China put the CBAM bill under such reshuffling at roughly half of what unchanged trade flows would pay [@Sandbag2024]. The practice has a name from California's electricity market, where importers could swap in contracts for low-carbon power, a problem studied by @Bushnell2014. The World Bank's CBAM exposure work notes that exporting steel plants may be cleaner than those serving the home market [@Maliszewska2025].

**A worked example shows the arithmetic (stylized).** An exporter makes 10 Mt of crude steel a year: 8 Mt by BF-BOF at 2.0 tCO₂/t and 2 Mt by scrap-EAF at 0.4 tCO₂/t, figures rounded from the IEA intensities above. Its emissions are 16.8 MtCO₂, an average of 1.68 tCO₂/t. It sells 1 Mt to the EU, a tenth of output, at a certificate price of €80/tCO₂, ignoring mark-ups and the free allocation adjustment as in 2034 (Table 1, Figure 1).

| Stylized exporter, 1 Mt sold to the EU | Exports from average mix | Exports from scrap-EAF only |
|---|---:|---:|
| Embodied carbon in EU-bound steel (MtCO₂) | 1.68 | 0.40 |
| Exporter's total emissions (MtCO₂) | 16.8 | 16.8 |
| CBAM charge, plant data (€ million) | 134 | 32 |
| CBAM charge, country-sector average (€ million) | 134 | 134 |
| Net feebate payment at €80/tCO₂ on EU-bound steel (€/t) | 0 | −102 (a rebate) |
| Price signal facing every tonne the exporter makes (€/tCO₂) | 80 | 80 |

: Table 1. Shuffling in a stylized steel exporter. All numbers are stylized; CBAM charges assume full phase-in, no mark-up and no free allocation adjustment. The feebate benchmark is the sector average, 1.68 tCO₂/t.

![Scrap shuffling in a stylized exporter (10 Mt of steel: 8 Mt BF-BOF at 2.0 tCO₂/t, 2 Mt scrap-EAF at 0.4 tCO₂/t; 1 Mt sold to the EU at €80/tCO₂). A: routing scrap-based steel to the EU cuts the embodied carbon the border sees by 76 percent. B: the exporter's emissions do not change. C: the CBAM charge falls from €134 million to €32 million on plant data, but not on a country-sector basis.](figures/fig1_scrap_shuffling.png){width=100%}

Three lessons follow. Shuffling cuts the charge by €102 million while emissions stay at 16.8 MtCO₂. A country-sector basis removes the gain, but on its own dilutes the incentive: cutting blast-furnace intensity lowers the charge only on the tenth that reaches Europe, about €8 per tonne of CO₂ abated. And a domestic feebate at €80 restores the full incentive on every tonne, yet under the draft its EU-bound scrap steel shows a negative price paid and earns nothing.

**Scrap is scarce, so its low intensity is partly borrowed.** Scrap supply is fixed in the short run by what was scrapped years ago. Sending more of it into EU-bound steel leaves less for other uses, which are then met with ore-based steel. The reported fall in embodied carbon is largely a relabeling of who uses the scrap. The same holds for aluminum: country defaults for unwrought aluminum (CN 7601) run from 0.36 tCO₂/t for South Korea and Ukraine to 3.0 for China [@EC2025DefaultValues], and remelted scrap carries a small fraction of primary metal's emissions.

**Current rules recognize the risk but do not enforce against it.** The Regulation requires the Commission to monitor resource shuffling, without an enforcement mechanism [@Sandbag2024]. The Commission's December 2025 proposal adds artificial adjustment of supply chains to the list of circumvention practices [@EC2025Downstream]. Detecting intent plant by plant will be hard. Removing the reward is easier.

# One fix for both: measure the price signal by country and sector

**Recognize the relative carbon price alongside the price paid.** Keep the price paid as the basis of the Article 9 deduction, since it prevents double charging. Add the price signal, measured for the exporting country's sector as a whole, to the default carbon price. The TECP gives the method: it expresses any instrument, a tax, feebate, subsidy reform, performance standard or obligation, as the uniform carbon tax that would cut emissions by as much [@CFPB17]. It is the measurement that lets the border recognize what a feebate or a non-price instrument actually does.

**Offer non-punitive defaults to exporters with a sector-wide signal.** The submission's central proposal is a third route between plant data and punitive defaults: country-level default values without the mark-up, available where the exporting country runs a domestic relative carbon price in the sector [@Stretton2026Submission]. Credit would follow the additional costs the instrument imposes on producers, not only its net revenue, which lets a country rebate output. Under this route every tonne from the country is charged at the sector average, so routing earns nothing (Table 1, last column of the charge rows), while the domestic feebate gives every plant the full incentive. As the importer's charge rises, so does the exporter's best feebate rate [@CFPB11].

**Phase recognition of implicit and rebated pricing in from 2027 to 2034.** Measurement is uncertain, and the methodology needs time. A factor rising linearly from zero in 2027 to one in 2034 matches the phase-out of free allocation to EU producers, so recognition of foreign pricing strengthens as EU producers' exposure does. Both signs should count, so that a country reducing fuel subsidies sees its default rise with each annual update.

**Close the offsetting gaps.** The Commission should confirm that decarbonization support financed from carbon-pricing revenue, open to all producers, granted on application and aimed at cutting the recipient's emissions, does not reduce the recognized price, as the draft already implies [@ELP2026]. Such support pays for behavior rather than output, so it strengthens the signal. It should also withhold recognition where contemporaneous budget measures plainly offset the carbon price, and issue guidance on state-owned enterprises whose losses the state absorbs.

**Develop the two methodologies together.** The default carbon price and the default values are being built separately, and each can be gamed through the other. The default values are due for revision by December 2027; that revision is the natural point to adopt country-sector measurement for mixed-route exporters [@Stretton2026Submission].

**Two modest extensions go beyond the submission.** First, benchmarks could be set per product rather than per production route, so that the route assigned to a country does not itself reward scrap use. Second, scrap could be valued at its opportunity cost, the emissions of the ore-based steel that replaces it elsewhere, when a plant's scrap share for EU-bound output exceeds its historical share. Both need analysis before adoption.

# Limits

**The deepest tension cannot be fixed inside CBAM.** An economy-wide carbon price raises costs on all production, and CBAM can credit only the share sold to Europe. Exporters face a trilemma: equal carbon costs on all output, competitiveness in markets without a border adjustment, and WTO rules against destination-specific rebates cannot all hold under one instrument. The resolution is two instruments, a production feebate and a destination-based consumption charge [@CFPB11; @CFPB16].

**Some changes need the Regulation amended.** Article 9(4) admits a default carbon price only where the exporting country has set one, and nets rebates from it [@EU2025Omnibus]. Recognizing subsidy reform or a feebate's signal therefore needs either a broad reading of "compensation" or an amendment at the next review. Country-specific treatment also raises most-favored-nation questions that need legal analysis [@Mehling2019; @IsmerNeuhoff2007]. Generous, rebuttable defaults, as @Cosbey2019 and @KeenParryRoaf2022 recommend, reduce that risk.

# What to do

For the European Commission: publish the default carbon price methodology for a separate consultation, built on the World Bank, IMF and OECD measures rather than from scratch, country- and sector-specific and updated each year. Recognize the price signal, measured as a TECP, alongside the price paid, with implicit and rebated pricing phased in from 2027 to 2034. Offer country-level defaults without the mark-up to exporters with a sector-wide domestic carbon price. Confirm the treatment of revenue-financed decarbonization support, and guard against offsetting subsidies. Adopt country-sector measurement for mixed-route steel and aluminum exporters in the December 2027 default-value revision, and propose any needed amendment to Article 9 at the next review.

For exporting countries: a sector-wide feebate, with revenue returned as decarbonization support where needed, prices every tonne at a rate a tax could not reach, and is the instrument these changes would reward [@CFPB12].
